1	# The two hard stops
2	
3	Most of this skill assembles a package and reports what is missing. Two
4	conditions are different: they **block**, and no amount of user insistence
5	converts them into a warning.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Revision mismatch
10	
11	**The revision in the document library must match the revision on the ERP item
12	master. When they disagree, stop.**
13	
14	This is not a data-quality nicety. **Sending a supplier the wrong revision is
15	the classic and expensive error this skill exists to prevent**, and it is
16	expensive in a specific way: nothing goes wrong for months. The supplier quotes
17	the drawing you sent, wins the business, tools up, and ships parts that are
18	correct against the print in their hand and wrong against the one in yours. You
19	find out at first article if you are lucky, and at the customer if you are not.
20	
21	### What to check
22	
23	| Check | Where |
24	|---|---|
25	| Revision on the drawing file itself | The title block, not the filename. Filenames lie |
26	| Revision recorded in the document library | M365 metadata or the library's own record |
27	| Revision on the ERP item master | Where the profile's `### ERP scope` says revision lives: a named field, the item-ID suffix with its pattern, or not in the ERP. **Never inferred**: with no setting, say the ERP's revision location is not set and that the check could not use the ERP |
28	| Revision the current demand was ordered against | Open purchase orders and sales orders |
29	
30	**Read the title block, not the filename.** `4471-B-RevC-final-v2.pdf` tells you
31	what somebody typed. The title block tells you what the drawing is.
32	
33	### What to report
34	
35	Name both revisions, both sources, and both dates. Do not resolve it — this is
36	a controlled-document question with an owner, and that owner is not the skill.
37	
38	> *"Stopping before assembling the package. The document library holds
39	> 4471-B at Rev C, dated 2026-06-11. The NetSuite item master records Rev B, and
40	> the open demand on PO-8841 was placed against Rev B. Those cannot both be
41	> current. Either the item master was not updated when C released, or C was
42	> released and never flowed to purchasing.*
43	>
44	> *That distinction matters to the quote, because the two revisions differ. I
45	> need document control to confirm which revision this sourcing action is
46	> against before anything goes to a supplier."*
47	
48	### The one thing not to do
49	
50	Do not send both revisions and let the supplier work it out. It looks helpful. It
51	produces bids that are not comparable, and it tells the supplier that your
52	configuration control is unreliable, which is a bad thing for them to know while
53	they are pricing you.
54	
55	---
56	
57	## 2. Restricted data
58	
59	**ITAR, EAR, export-controlled, or otherwise restricted technical data must not
60	be assembled into an outbound package without an explicit gate.** This is
61	blocking, and it blocks before assembly rather than before sending.
62	
63	The reason for the ordering: once restricted geometry is collated into a package
64	that is one click from an email, the control has already been weakened. Stop at
65	the point of gathering.
66	
67	### How it shows up
68	
69	- An ITAR or EAR marking in the drawing title block or border
70	- A distribution statement, or "export controlled" in a document header
71	- A customer program known to be defence, space or controlled — captured in
72	  `## Plant context` during `onboarding`
73	- A supplier who is not on the plant's cleared list for that program
74	
75	### What to do
76	
77	Report it as blocking, name what was found and where, and state the specific
78	question that needs answering — usually whether the candidate supplier holds the
79	required registration and whether an export authorization covers the disclosure.
80	
81	**Do not assess eligibility.** Whether a given supplier may receive controlled
82	technical data is a compliance determination with a named owner at the plant. The
83	skill's job is to notice, stop, and route it there.
84	
85	---
86	
87	## Why these two and not the rest
88	
89	Everything else this skill finds goes on the missing-items list and the user
90	decides. These two are different because **both produce a harm that lands
91	somewhere other than where the mistake was made** — with a supplier who built to
92	the wrong print, or with a compliance exposure the plant carries.
93	
94	A missing lead-time requirement produces a worse bid, and that is visible
95	immediately. These two are not visible until much later, which is exactly why
96	they are gates rather than warnings.
97

1	# The response specification — making bids comparable by construction
2	
3	**The highest-leverage line in the whole package**, and the one most often left
4	out.
5	
6	---
7	
8	## The problem it solves
9	
10	Three suppliers reply to the same request in three shapes:
11	
12	| Supplier | What they sent |
13	|---|---|
14	| A | $4.10 per piece, tooling included, 6 weeks |
15	| B | $3,180 per lot of 1,000, tooling quoted separately at $8,500, "8–10 weeks ARO" |
16	| C | $3.85/pc at 1,000 and $3.40 at 5,000, tooling amortized over the first order, freight collect |
17	
18	Nobody can compare those. The buyer spends an afternoon normalising all three
19	onto one basis, guesses at the pieces that were not stated, and the comparison
20	they end up with is partly their own reconstruction rather than what the
21	suppliers actually offered.
22	
23	**Specifying the response format up front is what makes the later comparison
24	honest**, rather than a normalisation exercise performed after the fact by
25	somebody with an opinion about who should win.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## What to mandate
30	
31	### The bid structure
32	
33	- **Unit price at each stated quantity, separately.** Not an average, not a
34	  blended rate. One line per quantity break asked for.
35	- **Tooling and NRE priced separately**, never folded into the piece price. A
36	  supplier who buries $8,500 of tooling in the unit price at 1,000 looks
37	  expensive at 1,000 and cheap at 10,000, and the buyer cannot see why.
38	- **Tooling ownership stated.** Who owns it at the end matters as much as the
39	  price, and it decides whether a second source is even possible later.
40	- **Lead time, split into first article and production**, and stated from a
41	  named event — receipt of order, receipt of tooling approval — rather than "8
42	  weeks."
43	- **Minimum order quantity**, which frequently turns out to exceed the quantity
44	  quoted.
45	- **Currency**, explicitly.
46	- **Price validity period.**
47	- **Any exclusions or assumptions**, listed rather than implied. This is where
48	  the surprises live.
49	
50	### The commercial basis
51	
52	State the terms the bid must assume rather than letting each supplier assume
53	their own: **Incoterms or freight basis, packaging, payment terms.** Otherwise
54	one bid is delivered and another is ex-works, and the difference is invisible
55	until the invoice.
56	
57	### The response schedule
58	
59	- A **due date** for the response
60	- **Who to send it to**, and how
61	- A **named contact** for technical questions, with the note that answers given
62	  to one bidder will be shared with all — which is both fair and the thing that
63	  stops a scope drift nobody sees
64	
65	---
66	
67	## Say what happens to a non-conforming bid
68	
69	A required format that carries no consequence is a suggestion.
70	
71	State plainly that a bid returned in a different shape will be sent back for
72	restatement rather than normalised on the buyer's side. Most suppliers comply
73	immediately, because the request is reasonable and the alternative costs them
74	time too.
75	
76	---
77	
78	## Where the quantities come from
79	
80	The demand picture is what makes the bid meaningful, and it is worth being
81	accurate rather than optimistic.
82	
83	- **Historical usage**, over a stated window, from the ERP
84	- **Open demand** currently on the books
85	- **Forecast or estimated annual usage**, clearly labelled as a forecast
86	
87	**Suppliers price 100 a year very differently from 10,000 a year.** A quantity
88	quoted without a volume context gets priced defensively, and the plant pays for
89	that pessimism on every part.
90	
91	**Never inflate the forecast to get a better price.** It produces a price the
92	supplier cannot hold, and the renegotiation arrives at the worst possible moment
93	— usually once the alternate source has already been qualified and the leverage
94	has moved.
95	
96	Where usage history is unavailable or the part is new, **say so in the request**
97	rather than omitting the volume. "New part, no usage history, initial order 500,
98	annual volume not yet established" is a statement a supplier can price against.
99	Silence is not, and they will assume the worst.
100	
101	---
102	
103	## When the bids come back
104	
105	Each returned bid is read into `../../../shared/contracts/supplier-bid.md`,
106	which mirrors the bid structure above field for field. A field the supplier did
107	not supply is listed in `fields_missing`, and the restatement request names it.
108	Read `bid-comparison.md`.
109

2	
3	Steps 11 to 13. The returned bids go into one shape, the comparison is
4	computed from that shape, and the buyer decides. The shape is
5	`../../../shared/contracts/supplier-bid.md`; the format the package asked for
6	is `bid-comparability.md`.
7

9	
10	## Step 11 — Ingest each bid
11	
12	Bids arrive as a PDF, an email, a spreadsheet, or pasted text. Read each into a
13	supplier bid record, **one per response**, every value with its `source_ref`.
14	
15	**Map, never normalise.** The record holds what the supplier stated:
16	
17	- **A lot price is not a unit price.** *"$410 for 200"* goes in `as_quoted`
18	  and `unit_price` stays null. Dividing it is the buyer's afternoon of
19	  normalising that the mandated format exists to remove.
20	- **Tooling folded into the piece price** is `tooling_in_unit_price: true`,
21	  not a tooling price of zero.
22	- **"About a week"** is not a lead time from a named event. Keep the words,
23	  leave the split fields null.
24	- **Silence on the quality clauses** is `not_stated`, never accepted.
25	- **No currency stated** is null, never assumed.
26	- **A break the package asked for and the supplier did not price** stays on the
27	  record with nulls. It is the gap a buyer most needs to see.
28	
29	### Off-format bids
30	
31	A bid is `off_format` when any mandated field is missing or in another shape.
32	**List every field not supplied in `fields_missing`, by name**, by checking
33	each mandated field in turn — unit price at each break, currency, lead time
34	first article and production from a named event, tooling price or a statement
35	that none is needed, tooling ownership, MOQ, validity, quality clause
36	acceptance — not by noticing what stands out.
37	
38	Then draft a restatement request for the buyer to send, per
39	`bid-comparability.md`, *Say what happens to a non-conforming bid*: it names
40	the missing fields and asks for the bid in the package's format. It goes
41	between `=== SUPPLIER EMAIL — SENDABLE — <supplier> ===` (or `HELD`, per
42	`supplier-loop.md`) and `=== END ===`, and the outbound check there applies — **nothing about other bids**.
43	A restated bid gets a new `bid_ref` that `supersedes` the old one.
44	
45	A bid that claims to be from a supplier not on the candidate list is ingested,
46	marked `not_confirmed_approved`, and flagged.
47	
48	**Show every record in the reply** as the summary table in
49	`../../../shared/replies.md` — supplier, source file, the break prices as
50	quoted, `fields_missing` by that name — and save the full record. The buyer
51	reads the reply, and a record that exists only in a file nobody opened has not
52	been shown; a raw YAML block is shown but not read.
53

56	## Step 12 — Compare, in code
57	
58	**Every figure in the comparison is computed by code over the bid records**
59	and printed from the result, with a figures block per
60	`../../../shared/computed-figures.md`. No price is retyped from a PDF into the
61	table.
62	
63	### One table per quantity break
64	
65	| Supplier | Approval | Unit price | Extended (unit × qty) | Tooling | MOQ | Lead time FA / production | Clauses | Exceptions | Validity | Readiness | Source |
66	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
67	
68	- **Readiness** is the derived status from step 13, *ready for buyer review*
69	  or *provisional* with what is open, in the same table.
70	  There is no second full table repeating approval, readiness or open
71	  requirements; the per-prerequisite evidence sits in the detail below,
72	  collapsible, never removed.
73	
74	- **Extended** is unit price × break quantity, computed. A bid with no unit
75	  price at that break reads *not quoted per unit*, with `as_quoted` beside it;

78	- **First-order total** — extended plus one-time tooling — gets its own column

2	
3	**Emitted by** `supplier-quote-request`, when a returned bid is ingested (step 11), and when the buyer states a decision (step 13)
4	**Consumed by** `supplier-quote-request` at the comparison (step 12), and `quote-build` at the cost buildup, where the awarded bid becomes a sourced outside-processing line
5	**Chain** 5, and any sourcing event a quote started
6	**Contract version** 1
7	
8	Rules that govern every contract are in [README.md](README.md).
9	
10	---
11	
12	## What this carries
13	
14	**Two records, each written whole at its own emit time.**
15	
16	1. **The supplier bid** — one per supplier response, written when the bid is
17	   ingested. It mirrors the mandated response format the package asked for
18	   (`../../skills/supplier-quote-request/reference/bid-comparability.md`), so a
19	   conforming bid fills every field and an off-format bid shows exactly where
20	   it fell short.
21	2. **The selection record** — one per sourcing event, written when the buyer
22	   tells the skill which bid they chose. **The buyer decides; the skill records
23	   it.** A recommendation is never a selection record.
24	
25	**Every value is what the supplier stated, with where they stated it.** A bid
26	that quoted a lot price has no unit price on this record. A bid that said
27	nothing about the quality clauses has not accepted them. Per
28	`../absent-is-not-zero.md`, a field the supplier did not supply is null and
29	listed in `fields_missing`, never zero, never a default, never "probably
30	included."
31	
32	**Both records are internal.** Nothing on them goes to any supplier: not the
33	prices, not the other bidders' names, not the ranking. Per
34	`../secret-config.md`, *The outbound document check*.
35	
36	---

1	# Quality clauses, and the suppliers who can meet them
2	
3	---
4	
5	## The clause list
6	
7	The requirements a supplier must meet to be allowed to ship this part. They are
8	part of the price — a supplier quoting without them is quoting a different job —
9	so they belong in the request rather than in the purchase order afterwards.
10	
11	| Clause | What it obliges the supplier to do |
12	|---|---|
13	| Certification | Hold a current registration to the applicable standard — ISO 9001 general, AS9100 aerospace, IATF 16949 automotive |
14	| Material certification | Supply mill certs traceable to the heat or lot |
15	| First article inspection | Submit a full dimensional report on the first production part before running the balance |
16	| PPAP submission | The automotive production-part approval package, at a stated submission level. **The level changes the cost materially** |
17	| Certificate of conformance | Ship with a signed statement of conformance per lot |
18	| Right of access | Permit audits by us, our customer, and the regulator |
19	| Change notification | Notify before changing process, sub-tier supplier, or location |
20	| Record retention | Hold records for a stated period |
21	| Lot traceability | Maintain lot identity through their process, which is what makes ours possible |
22	
23	**PPAP level is not a detail.** Level 1 is a warrant; level 3 is a full package
24	with dimensional results, material and performance test results, process flow,
25	PFMEA and control plan. Quoting the wrong level is a real and unpleasant cost
26	surprise, and it is one of the more common ones.
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Revision matters as much here as on the drawing
31	
32	**Quote against the clause list at its current revision.** A superseded clause
33	list produces bids that are not valid, in exactly the way a superseded drawing
34	does — and it is far less likely that anyone notices, because nobody reads the
35	clause list twice.
36	
37	Where the clause set captured during `onboarding` is unavailable, **list the
38	clauses found on the current part record and flag the whole set as unverified.**
39	Do not assemble a plausible standard list from what plants usually require. A
40	confidently wrong clause list is worse than an admitted gap, because the buyer
41	will not re-check it.
42	
43	---
44	
45	## Clauses vary by customer program — surface it, never merge it
46	
47	The same part number can carry different requirements depending on which
48	customer's program it is being built for. One customer flows down AS9100 plus a
49	level-3 PPAP; another takes the same part under ISO 9001 with a certificate of
50	conformance.
51	
52	**Surface the variation and let the buyer decide.** Do not merge the sets.
53	
54	Merging fails in both directions and both are bad: take the union and you have
55	quoted the most expensive requirements onto every unit, so the price is wrong
56	and the plant loses money quietly forever. Take the intersection and you have
57	sourced parts that cannot legally ship to the stricter customer, which is a
58	nonconformance you have manufactured on purpose.
59	
60	---
61	
62	## Candidate suppliers
63	
64	Existing qualified suppliers for this commodity, from the ERP vendor
65	records, plus the current supplier for comparison.
66	
67	Where the trigger was a supplier-caused flag, the implicated supplier stays on
68	the list, clearly marked. The buyer needs to see the incumbent's price next to
69	the alternates, and sometimes the answer is a corrective action with the
70	incumbent rather than a switch.
71	
72	### Single-source risk is the finding
73	
74	**If exactly one qualified supplier exists, flag it loudly.** That is usually
75	more important than the sourcing package it appeared in.
76	
77	A part with one qualified supplier means a quality problem at that supplier
78	stops production, with no path around it. Sourcing an alternate is insurance,
79	and the moment you discover you need it is the moment it is too late to get it —
80	which is precisely why Chain 5 exists.
81	
82	### Requalification lead time is why starting early is the value
83	
84	An alternate supplier cannot simply start shipping. They have to be qualified:
85	sample parts, first article inspection, often a full PPAP, sometimes a site
86	audit. **Weeks to months.**
87	
88	State the expected requalification path with the candidate list, so nobody reads
89	an alternate source as available next month. The whole argument for starting a
90	sourcing action off the back of a quality finding is that the clock is long and
91	it has just started.

5

7	tracks and compares. It never sends, never awards, and never decides that a
8	supplier who went quiet has dropped out.

12	## Step 8 — The candidate list
13	
14	### Where candidates come from

17	   `onboarding` (format in `../../onboarding/reference/config-profile.md`,

1	# Computed figures — a number is printed, never retyped
2	
3	**Shared across the plugin.** Every skill that reports a number follows this.
4	
5	The failure this exists to stop has one shape. The skill does the work
6	correctly, then writes the summary from memory. The summary says "eleven
7	maintenance records" where the data holds six, "3.1× the control limit" where
8	the division gives 2.36, "five orders" where the file has six — the customer's
9	own order being the one missed. Each figure is stated with total confidence,
10	and each is the first thing a quality manager or an estimator will check.
11	
12	A second shape sits next to it: the confident absence. "The sister machine has
13	no bearing history." "There is no PM plan in the library." Said after one
14	search, about a record that was there.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## The rule
19	
20	**Every count, total, ratio, percentage and "N of M" in user-facing output is
21	produced by code run over the data in this session, and printed from that
22	result. A number is never retyped, rounded from memory, or paraphrased.**
23	
24	**A negative claim — "has no history," "no plan exists," "not in the file" —
25	cites the exact query or filter that returned nothing.** Where the search tool
26	may be incomplete (SharePoint search under-reports), enumerate the folder
27	instead, or say *"not found by search"* rather than *"does not exist."* Those
28	are different claims and only the first one was earned.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## The figures block — a required part of the output
33	
34	A rule that says "check your numbers" is a rule nobody can see being skipped.
35	So the check is an output, not an intention.
36	
37	**Every run that reports a number emits a figures block**, produced by code,
38	before the prose that uses it. One row per figure:
39	
40	| Figure | Value | Computed from | Filter or query |
41	|---|---|---|---|
42	| Maintenance records, HAAS-VF4-02 | 9 | maintenance export | `asset_id == "HAAS-VF4-02"` |
43	| Sibling records mentioning "bearing" | 2 (LMB-13781, LMB-14022, both HAAS-VF4-05) | maintenance export | same model, `notes` contains "bearing" |
44	| Measured ÷ upper control limit | 1.87 | inspection export | measured and limit both from the same computation |
45	| PM plan documents found | 0 — **not found by search** | M365 library | search "PM plan"; folder not enumerated |
46	
47	Then three things hold, and a reader can check all three without re-running
48	anything:
49	
50	1. **The prose quotes the block.** A number that appears in the narrative, a
51	   table or a headline appears in the block with the same value. A number in
52	   the prose with no row in the block is a defect.
53	2. **A ratio comes from the same computation as its parts.** Do not compute a
54	   control limit in code and then divide by it in your head.
55	3. **A subtotal reconciles to its total in the block itself.** If 126 records
56	   matched, the exact and normalized rows add to 126, and each equals the sum
57	   of the classes it is made of. A block that does not add up is fixed before
58	   anything is written from it.
59	
60	Where the skill already emits "the structured data behind the report," the
61	figures block is part of it. Where the output is a controlled document going to
62	a customer or supplier, the block stays on the internal side.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## When no code can be run
67	
68	Some sessions have no code execution. Then the count was made by reading, and
69	the output says so: **"counted by reading, not computed — verify before
70	relying on it,"** on the block and beside any figure that matters. Never
71	present a hand count as a computed one. This is `absent-is-not-zero.md` applied
72	to the method rather than the data: an unverified number named as unverified is
73	useful, and one dressed as computed is worse than none.
74	
75	---
76	
77	## What this does not change
78	
79	- A figure that cannot be read is still reported unreadable. The block carries
80	  the row with the reason, never a guess.
81	- Rates, whether read from an `MFG_*` variable or the plant profile, follow
82	  `secret-config.md`. The block names the source; the value appears only where
83	  the audience rule allows.
84	- Computing a figure is not applying a fix. Anything that changes data still
85	  needs its yes.
